title: Response of the Office of Structured Finance, Division of Corporation Finance, to Latham & Watkins LLP regarding certain data center securitizations
date_evidence: July 29, 2026 / Response of the Office of Structured Finance / Division of Corporation Finance
key_claim: SEC staff agree that, on the facts represented, securities issued in data-centre securitisations are not asset-backed securities as defined in section 3(a)(79) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, and note the letter has no legal force or effect.
frame_summary: This source is arguing a narrow definitional point: on the represented structure, the issuer's direct ownership of the facilities takes these securities outside the statutory asset-backed definition, and staff decline to create any obligation beyond that.
verbatim_quote: Based on the representations in your letter, we agree that the fixed-income or other securities issued in data center securitizations of the type described in your letter are not asset-backed securities as defined in section 3(a)(79) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934.
verbatim_list: This letter, like all staff statements, has no legal force or effect: it does not alter or amend applicable law, and it creates no new or additional obligations for any person.
notes: Primary document. Reported in secondary coverage as an 'exemption' dated August 2026; both framings are wrong. It is a staff interpretive letter dated 29 July 2026. publisher: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (Division of Corporation Finance, Office of Structured Finance)
title: Incoming request for interpretive guidance regarding certain data center securitizations, submitted by Latham & Watkins LLP
date_evidence: July 23, 2026 / Office of Structured Finance / Division of Corporation Finance
key_claim: The requesting letter describes the standard structure: an anticipated repayment date of approximately five years against a final maturity of 25-30 years, with a loan-to-value ratio not exceeding 70% of appraised value at issuance.
frame_summary: This source is arguing that data-centre securitisations resemble single-asset commercial real-estate financings rather than pools of receivables, and should therefore sit outside the asset-backed securities definition.
verbatim_quote: The securities typically have an anticipated repayment date of approximately five years and a final maturity of 25-30 years.
verbatim_list: The securities are generally structured with a loan-to-value ratio not exceeding 70% of the appraised value of the Securitized Assets at the time of issuance, with the remaining 30% of appraised value representing equity ownership, directly or indirectly, in the Asset Entity.
notes: Hosted on sec.gov as the incoming letter to the staff response. The cleanest primary tenor figures in the evidence base, and they sit inside a document arguing for lighter treatment.

key_claim: The FPC judges that debt maturities aligned with the asset life of AI chips would imply shorter tenors than most credit investors prefer, and that the scale of the resulting maturity mismatch, and its allocation across lenders, borrowers or tenants, depends on the terms of the debt agreements.
frame_summary: This source is arguing that the AI buildout's financing structure, not its demand assumptions alone, is the financial-stability variable, and that supervisors cannot judge the exposure without seeing the contract terms that allocate it.
verbatim_quote: The scale of this maturity mismatch risk across the debt financing of data centre facilities and AI chips, and how that risk is allocated across lenders, borrowers or tenants, will depend on the terms of the debt agreements.

The five AI hyperscalers accounted for just 3% of the stock of outstanding US IG debt at the end of 2025, but as of early May accounted for over 15% of year-to-date issuance.

title: Finance Advisory: SEC releases guidance on data center securitizations
key_claim: Because the securities fall outside the asset-backed definition, sponsors are not required to retain a 5% economic interest under the credit risk retention rules implementing Section 941 of Dodd-Frank.

title: SFA Research Corner: How data center ABS and CMBS fit in a broader financing ecosystem
key_claim: On Barclays figures, outstanding data-centre securitisation has grown from $4 billion in 2020 to $61 billion year-to-date 2026, and could reach $180 billion by end-2028, roughly 20% of the esoteric ABS market and 15% of the SASB CMBS market.
frame_summary: This source is arguing that securitisation is a takeout channel for already-stabilised, leased assets rather than the primary funding source for the buildout, so its growth should not be read as construction-risk transfer.
verbatim_quote: According to Barclays Research, outstanding issuance has grown from $4 billion in 2020 to $61 billion year-to-date 2026, reflecting the growing role of securitization in financing stabilized data-center assets.
verbatim_list: Barclays projects that if outstanding data-center securitizations reach $180 billion by year-end 2028, they could comprise roughly 20% of the esoteric ABS market and 15% of the SASB CMBS market.

Morgan Stanley estimates that global investment in data centers—including land, buildings, power infrastructure and computing hardware—will require approximately $2.9 trillion in capital expenditures through 2028.
notes: Industry association, so Tier 3 under the rubric. Headline figures are third-party estimates (Barclays, Morgan Stanley) restated by SFA and cited as such. Contains no numeric lease-tenor figure.

title: How worried should we be about AI debt? (Stefan Hepp)
date_evidence: - By Stefan Hepp - August 07, 2026 - CBR - Finance
key_claim: A stress test of the AI financing complex finds first-loss positions sitting mostly outside the regulated banking system and aggregate credit losses smaller and less concentrated than in 2008-09, though refinancing at maturity and vendor guarantees remain weak points.
frame_summary: This source is arguing that AI-related credit exposure is unlikely to produce a 2008-style banking crisis because the first-loss layer sits with non-bank investors, which is the strongest available case against reading the mismatch as systemic.
verbatim_quote: A decline in market capitalization does not cause bonds to default, and a data center with a financially sound tenant can service its debt through a tech-sector sell-off.
verbatim_list: The results of this test suggest that today's situation is not a rerun of the 2008–09 financial crisis: First-loss positions sit mostly outside the regulated banking system.
notes: Counter-evidence. The same article flags refinancing at maturity and vendor-guarantee fragility, so it is genuinely two-sided rather than a hedge. title: Powering progress: financing the infrastructure behind US data center growth
key_claim: A $4.25 billion senior secured notes offering was 100% pre-leased under a 15-year triple-net lease to a high investment-grade tenant, which the bank presents as evidence of underwriting discipline rather than speculative excess.
frame_summary: This source is arguing that long contracted leases to investment-grade tenants make the sector's debt conservatively underwritten, which is the market's own answer to the mismatch question.
